name: Johann Sebastian Bach
alt: An oil painting of an older man in 18th-century dress with a powdered wig, holding a rolled sheet of music.
facts: He wrote a brand-new piece of music almost every single week for years while working as a church choirmaster in Germany.
He had over 20 children, and several of them grew up to become composers too.
He once walked roughly 250 miles, mostly on foot, just to hear another organist play.

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
alt: An oil painting of a young man with powdered hair and a red coat, gazing slightly sideways.
facts: He was composing his own music before he turned 5 years old.
He secretly copied down a piece of church music from memory after hearing it performed just once, even though copying it was forbidden.
He could compose an entire piece in his head before ever putting pen to paper.

name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
alt: An old engraved portrait of a bearded man in a long dark robe.
facts: He spent most of his career as the music director at one of the most important churches in Rome.
His smooth, calm style of choral writing became the model that church composers were told to imitate for centuries afterward.
Legend credits him with saving elaborate church polyphony from being banned outright by leaders who worried the words were getting lost in the music.

name: George Frideric Handel
alt: An oil painting of a heavyset man in a powdered wig and dark coat, facing forward.
facts: He wrote one of his most famous works, about the life of Jesus, in only about three weeks.
He moved from Germany to England and became so beloved there that he's buried in a hall reserved for the country's national heroes.
Audiences have stood up during one particular chorus of his ever since a king supposedly did the same.

name: Antonio Vivaldi
alt: An old engraving of a man with curly red hair playing a violin.
facts: He was ordained as a priest but became so famous for music that people nicknamed him after his red hair instead of his collar.
He taught violin at an orphanage for girls for most of his career, writing much of his most famous music for his students to perform.
He wrote more than 500 concertos, including a famous set inspired by the four seasons of the year.

name: Gabriel Fauré
alt: A black-and-white photo of an older man with a thick white mustache and beard.
facts: He spent over 15 years as the organist at a grand church in Paris while writing music on the side.
One of his most famous choral works was written for a funeral, but he said he wanted it to feel peaceful rather than frightening.
He eventually became the director of one of France's top music schools, after years of supporting himself mainly by teaching piano.

name: Franz Schubert
alt: An oil painting of a young man with curly hair and small round glasses.
facts: He wrote more than 600 songs in a lifetime that lasted only 31 years.
He set a famous prayer to music so beautifully that it's still sung at weddings and funerals two centuries later.
He was so shy about sharing his own music that many of his greatest works weren't performed in public until after he had died.

name: Tomás Luis de Victoria
alt: An old engraved portrait of a man in a plain clerical collar.
facts: He left his home country to study for the priesthood in Rome, where he also became one of the leading composers of his time.
He spent his final years as chaplain to a dowager empress, writing sacred music for her private chapel.
His choral music is still sung in churches today, written entirely for voices alone, with no instruments at all.

name: Gregorio Allegri
alt: An old painting of a man in dark religious robes with a white collar.
facts: He wrote a piece for the Sistine Chapel that the Pope decreed could never be copied or performed anywhere else.
For over a century, the only way to hear his most famous work was to travel to Rome during Holy Week.
A teenage visitor is famously said to have broken the secrecy by listening to it twice and writing the whole thing down from memory.

name: Johannes Brahms
alt: A black-and-white photo of an older man with a long white beard and round glasses.
facts: He took over 20 years to finish his first symphony because he felt so much pressure to live up to earlier German composers.
He wrote a large-scale choral work to comfort the living after losing his mother and his mentor in the same year, rather than focusing on judgment day like older requiems did.
He had a reputation for being gruff and blunt in person, even though his music is full of warmth.

name: Giuseppe Verdi
alt: A black-and-white photo of an older man with a thick white beard, looking off to the side.
facts: He's best known for his operas, but he also wrote a dramatic Requiem so theatrical that one famous conductor called it 'an opera in church robes.'
He grew up the son of a village innkeeper and almost failed the entrance exam to the music conservatory in Milan.
He donated much of his fortune to build a retirement home for musicians who had fallen on hard times.

name: Charles Gounod
alt: An old sepia-toned photo of a man with long gray hair and a thick beard.
facts: He once seriously considered becoming a priest before deciding to dedicate his life to music instead.
His most famous melody was written as a tribute layered on top of a keyboard piece written by another composer a century earlier.
He composed an opera based on a famous tragic love story that's still one of the most performed operas in the world.

name: César Franck
alt: A black-and-white photo of an elderly man with glasses and a long white beard.
facts: He worked for over 30 years as the organist of a single Paris church, playing for services nearly every week.
He didn't become widely famous as a composer until very late in life, after decades known mainly as a teacher.
One of his most beloved pieces was written simply enough for an amateur church choir to sing, using just voice, harp, cello, and organ.

name: Maurice Duruflé
alt: A black-and-white photo of a young man with dark, neatly combed hair.
facts: He was such a perfectionist that he published only a small handful of works in his entire career, revising pieces for years before letting them go.
He based one of his most famous works almost entirely on ancient chant melodies that monks have sung for over a thousand years.
He worked for over four decades as the organist of the same Paris church, a job he only gave up after a serious car accident.

name: John Rutter
alt: A color photo of an older man with white hair, smiling warmly.
facts: He turned down a job leading a famous choir at Cambridge so he'd have more time to compose.
Choirs around the world perform his music every December, even though his most famous Christmas carols are entirely original, not old folk tunes.
He started his own small choir specifically so he could hear his own choral music performed exactly the way he imagined it.

name: Eric Whitacre
alt: A color photo of a man with short, light-colored hair against a dark background.
facts: He didn't learn to read music until college, after starting out as a music major who could barely play piano.
He brought together thousands of singers from dozens of countries who had never met in person, using nothing but webcams and the internet.
He says the spark that made him fall in love with choral music was joining a college choir almost by accident.

name: Ralph Vaughan Williams
alt: A black-and-white photo of a middle-aged man with thick eyebrows and tousled hair.
facts: He traveled the English countryside with a notebook, collecting old folk songs before they could be forgotten, and wove their melodies into his own music.
He helped edit a hymn book still used in churches today, and wrote one of its best-loved tunes himself.
He kept composing well into his 80s, finishing a symphony just a couple of years before he died.

name: Felix Mendelssohn
alt: An oil painting of a young man with dark curly hair and sideburns.
facts: He was such a musical prodigy that he wrote a piece still performed today by the time he was 17.
He's credited with reviving interest in a much earlier composer's work after organizing a performance of a piece that had been mostly forgotten for about a century.
He composed the tune millions of people sing every December without realizing it first celebrated the invention of the printing press, not Christmas.

name: Hildegard of Bingen
alt: An illuminated manuscript painting of a robed woman seated in an arched doorway, with flames above her head, dictating to a monk.
facts: She was running a religious community by her early 30s and is one of the earliest composers in history whose name we actually know.
She wrote her own original chant melodies, an unusually creative thing for someone in her position at the time, when most music was anonymous.
She also wrote about medicine, theology, and natural science, and described visions she said she'd had since childhood.

name: Claudio Monteverdi
alt: An oil painting of a man with a long gray beard, dressed in dark robes.
facts: He helped invent a brand-new kind of musical storytelling that eventually grew into what we now call opera.
He wrote an enormous setting of evening prayers that calls for multiple choirs, soloists, and instrumental groups all at once.
Late in life, after losing his wife, he became a priest while continuing to compose some of his most ambitious music.

name: Josquin des Prez
alt: An old woodcut portrait of a man wearing a round cap, shown inside a circular frame.
facts: Other composers of his era admired him so much that they wrote pieces specifically imitating his style, as a kind of tribute.
Music historians often credit him with making Renaissance vocal music feel truly expressive, rather than just technically clever.
A leading music printer of the time devoted entire songbooks to just his work, an honor almost no other composer received during his lifetime.

name: Orlande de Lassus
alt: An old oil portrait of a balding man in dark clothing with a ruffled collar.
facts: He was so famous in his own lifetime that a Pope made him a knight in recognition of his music.
He wrote more than 2,000 pieces in nearly every style and language popular in his era.
He spent over 30 years working for the same royal court in Germany, eventually becoming its most celebrated employee.

name: William Byrd
alt: An old engraved portrait of a bearded man with curly hair and a ruffled collar, shown inside a circular frame.
facts: He wrote music for two very different, sometimes dangerous religious communities at once, composing quietly for one faith while officially serving the other.
He held a rare legal monopoly that let him control music printing across his entire country for years.
He's remembered as one of the finest keyboard composers of his time, even though he's best known today for his choral music.

name: Guillaume Dufay
alt: A colorful medieval illustration of a robed man in a red cap, standing beside a small pipe organ.
facts: He was so renowned in his lifetime that a king and several dukes competed to employ him.
He helped develop musical techniques that composers kept building on for the next century.
He asked for two of his own pieces to be sung at his deathbed, and singers gathered to grant his wish.

name: Dietrich Buxtehude
alt: An old painting showing a man playing a viola da gamba alongside other musicians.
facts: A famous younger composer once walked for days just to spend a few months studying with him.
He spent decades as the organist of a major church in northern Germany, where his performances drew huge crowds.
He's remembered today mostly for his bold, dramatic organ music, even though he also wrote vocal works for his church.

name: Marc-Antoine Charpentier
alt: A small, faded old engraving of a curly-haired man, shown inside an oval frame.
facts: One of his short instrumental pieces became famous centuries later as the fanfare introducing a major international television broadcast.
He worked for a powerful French duchess for nearly 20 years, writing most of his major works for her household chapel.
Much of his music was nearly lost forever, staying unpublished in private manuscripts for over a century after his death.

name: Arvo Pärt
alt: A photo of an older bald man with a full beard, smiling and shown in profile.
facts: He invented his own simple, bell-like composing style only after years of feeling frustrated and going silent as a composer for most of a decade.
His music has been used in major films and dance performances worldwide, even though much of it was written for church choirs.
He grew up under a government that restricted religious music, so for years his sacred works could only be performed in secret or abroad.

name: Morten Lauridsen
alt: A color photo of an older man with a long gray beard, looking off to the side near a lake.
facts: He spent decades teaching composition at a West Coast university while quietly becoming one of the most performed choral composers alive.
One of his most beloved choral works was inspired by foggy walks near his cabin on a small island.
He received a major national arts medal from a U.S. president for his contribution to choral music.

name: Ola Gjeilo
alt: A color close-up photo of a smiling bald man with a beard, looking to the side.
facts: He moved from Northern Europe to the United States as a teenager specifically to study film scoring and composition.
His choral pieces are now some of the most frequently performed contemporary works by choirs around the world.
He often performs his own piano improvisations alongside choirs in concert, blending a classical choral sound with a more cinematic style.

name: James MacMillan
alt: A color photo of a smiling man with short gray hair, wearing a casual collared shirt.
facts: He once wrote a major orchestral work inspired by witch trials that took place in his home country centuries earlier.
He founded his own summer music festival in rural Scotland to bring world-class performances to a small local audience.
He was invited to compose music performed at the wedding of a future king and queen of his home country.

name: Fanny Mendelssohn
alt: An oil painting of a young woman with dark curly hair styled in ringlets, wearing a lace collar.
facts: She wrote hundreds of pieces of music in her lifetime, but her family discouraged her from publishing most of them because she was a woman.
Her own brother, a famous composer himself, sometimes performed her songs in public without telling the audience who had actually written them.
She finally began publishing music under her own name just a year before she died suddenly at the piano.

name: Clara Schumann
alt: A black-and-white photo of a young woman with center-parted hair, wearing a dark Victorian dress.
facts: She began touring Europe as a celebrated concert pianist while still a child, years before she ever published a note of her own music.
She raised eight children largely on her own while continuing to perform and compose, after her husband, also a famous composer, became seriously ill.
She kept performing into her 70s and became one of the first people to teach at a major German music conservatory.

name: Lili Boulanger
alt: A black-and-white photo of a young woman with short dark hair and bangs, wearing a lace-trimmed collar.
facts: She became the first woman ever to win one of the most prestigious composition prizes in her country, beating out male competitors twice her age.
She battled chronic illness for almost her entire life and died before turning 25, racing to finish her last major work from her sickbed.
Her older sister was also a respected composer, and the two grew up surrounded by some of the most famous musicians of their era.

name: Amy Beach
alt: An old black-and-white photo of a woman with hair pulled back, gazing directly at the camera.
facts: She became the first woman in her country to have a large-scale symphony performed by a major orchestra.
She largely taught herself composition by studying scores, since her husband didn't want her taking formal lessons after their marriage.
After her husband died, she kept touring as a concert pianist well into her 60s, performing her own works across the country.

name: Florence Price
alt: A sepia-toned studio photo of a woman with curled gray hair, wearing pearl earrings.
facts: She became the first Black woman in her country to have a symphony she wrote performed by a major orchestra.
She sometimes submitted her compositions to contests without revealing her race, fearing it would keep her music from even being considered.
For decades after her death, boxes of her unpublished scores sat forgotten in an old house until they were rediscovered by chance.

name: Margaret Bonds
alt: A black-and-white photo of a woman with short curled hair, smiling gently at the camera.
facts: She was mentored as a teenager by an older woman composer who became one of her closest lifelong friends and collaborators.
She set the words of a famous poet of her era to music so often that their two names are still closely linked today.
She was one of the first Black musicians to perform as a soloist with a major American symphony orchestra.

name: Caroline Shaw
alt: A color photo of a woman with shoulder-length wavy hair, smiling outdoors.
facts: She became the youngest person ever to win one of the most prestigious prizes in American music composition.
She still regularly performs as a violinist and singer in addition to composing, often in the same concerts as her own pieces.
Her breakout piece for eight voices uses no instruments at all, just close harmony and unconventional vocal sounds.

name: Errollyn Wallen
alt: A color photo of a smiling woman with natural hair, seated near a piano.
facts: She wrote a piece performed live at the opening ceremony of a major international sporting event watched by billions of people.
She left a science degree to retrain as a dancer before eventually turning to composing and performing her own songs.
She was honored by her adopted country's monarchy for her services to music.

name: Joan Tower
alt: A color close-up photo of a smiling older woman with short hair.
facts: She wrote a series of fanfares directly answering a much older, more famous set of fanfares honoring a different kind of person.
She played percussion in her own new-music ensemble for over a decade before focusing on composing full time.
She became the first woman to win one of the most significant prizes in American orchestral composition.

name: Libby Larsen
alt: A color photo of a smiling older woman with short gray hair, captured mid-applause.
facts: She co-founded one of the first composer-run organizations in her country dedicated to helping composers get their orchestral works performed.
She has written more than 15 operas, along with hundreds of other pieces across nearly every musical genre.
One of her works was inspired by the letters and diary entries of a famous frontier-era woman.
